Inversion addresses a widely underestimated problem: Agents tend to start generating too early. When a user says "help me design a system," the Agent immediately draws architecture, chooses a database, lists services—looks complete, but in fact none of the key constraints have been confirmed. The Inversion pattern reverses the process, forcing the Agent to first act as an interviewer: first clarify the problem, user, and scale, then ask about deployment environment, tech stack, and non-negotiable constraints; do not proceed to final solution synthesis until the phase is complete. The core here is the gating mechanism—"ask if needed" is not enough, as the Agent tends to think it already knows; defining phases, exit conditions, and when to stop are what make the design reliable. The Pipeline pattern targets the problem of skipping steps in complex tasks. Document generation, release, data migration, code refactoring, and incident retrospectives all require inventory first, then generation, then confirmation, then assembly, then quality inspection. The key to Pipeline is the checkpoint mechanism—do not generate an architecture plan until requirements are fully asked, do not generate the final document until the API list is confirmed, do not claim the fix is complete until tests have passed, do not enter release recommendations until risk items are graded, and do not execute destructive operations without confirmation. Once such gating becomes vague, the Agent can easily fill in subsequent steps on its own and directly output results that appear complete but are actually unverified.
